measurement.happened:
This week in DR Congo was dominated by three major threads: a worsening Ebola crisis, a bold constitutional power grab by President Tshisekedi, and continued bloodshed in the east.

Ebola remains the story of the week and arguably the biggest. Cases passed 11,000 with 5,387 deaths, making it the deadliest outbreak the country has seen, according to Al Jazeera and Reuters. MSF declared the outbreak still out of control after six months, and warned that millions of dollars in funding are going missing while the virus keeps spreading (BBC, Bloomberg, TV5Monde). The CDC and Africa CDC both flagged that attacks on health workers are actively hampering the response (Reuters, TV5Monde). Merck urged wider deployment of the Ervebo vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain (Bloomberg, TV5Monde). The outbreak is also hitting the economy: Barrick Gold furloughed some employees at its Congo mine as an Ebola precaution (Reuters), and a metals trader backed by quants is in talks to secure a tin deal, suggesting commodity markets are watching the outbreak closely (Bloomberg). On top of Ebola, Deutsche Welle reported the return of cholera, raising fears of a compounded health emergency. TV5Monde noted hundreds of millions of dollars have been poured into the response with visible gaps remaining.

On the political front, President Félix Tshisekedi signed a contested referendum law that opens the door to a new Constitution and, by extension, a third term in office (Reuters, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, BBC). Parliament had passed the law, and the move is seen as a constitutional gamble, as Bloomberg put it. The timing is notable because it lands while the country is in the middle of a major health crisis and ongoing wars in the east. In a related power play, the government announced it wants to rename streets and public places that bear the name of former president Joseph Kabila (TV5Monde), a symbolic erasure that is already sparking debate. Meanwhile, Lambert Mende, a former close ally of Kabila, publicly threw his support behind Tshisekedi (TV5Monde), signaling a shift in the political alliances around the president. The government also pushed to make Étienne Tshisekedi, Félix's late father, one of five national heroes, a move that is generating controversy (TV5Monde).

The military and conflict situation in the east remains grim. At least 66 Congolese soldiers were sentenced to death for what the authorities called cowardice and revolt before the enemy in the fight against FRN rebels (BBC, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde). Islamic State-affiliated ADF rebels killed at least 22 to 66 civilians in a single week in the east, including three health workers (AP, TV5Monde). BBC also carried a headline referencing M23 activity, suggesting the rebel landscape is multi-front. The death sentences for soldiers are a dramatic escalation in military discipline that will likely ripple through the armed forces.

At the Francophonie summit, DR Congo and Rwanda clashed over the leadership of the OIF. DRC proposed withdrawing its candidate and called on Rwanda to do the same, and signaled it was ready to back a Romanian candidate to block the Rwandan bid (TV5Monde, multiple dates). This is a proxy for the deeper RDC-Rwanda rivalry playing out in a multilateral setting. The summit became a stage for the two neighbors to jockey for influence among Francophone African states.

In lighter news, DR Congo played Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Comoros and Sierra Leone, with Watford midfielder Edo Kayembe scoring for the national team (BBC). A Reuters feature highlighted Congolese coders using AI to rescue school records lost to war, a small but human story. TV5Monde also ran a piece on DRC's ambition to transform its minerals domestically rather than exporting raw ore, signaling an industrial policy push.
measurement.expected:
Ebola will remain the dominant story next week. Almost certain: case numbers will continue to climb or at least hold above 11,000, and the death toll will tick upward. MSF and the CDC will keep issuing warnings about the pace of the outbreak. Possible: a new government press conference or emergency health council meeting to address the funding gaps MSF flagged. Unlikely: a sudden containment declaration; six months of spread and attacks on health workers make a quick turnaround improbable. The Barrick furlough and the tin-deal talks may generate follow-up reporting on how Ebola is reshaping mining operations.

The constitutional and political thread will keep moving. Almost certain: more public debate and media coverage of the referendum law and the third-term question, especially as the law is now signed and the process is formally underway. Possible: opposition parties or civil society groups organizing rallies or press conferences to contest the law. The Kabila street-renaming plan will likely provoke local pushback in cities where those streets are well known. The Lambert Mende defection to Tshisekedi's camp may draw further realignments among Kabila-era figures. Unlikely: a full-blown constitutional crisis or a snap vote within this single week; the referendum process takes time.

In the east, the fighting will continue. Probable: more ADF or FRN attacks in North Kivu or South Kivu, given the tempo of the past two weeks. The 66 death sentences for soldiers will generate more reporting and possibly appeals or internal army reactions. Possible: a new round of diplomatic shuffling, with the UN or AU commenting on the eastern conflict. The M23 thread mentioned by BBC could resurface if there is a new skirmish or a statement from the group.

At the Francophonie summit and in RDC-Rwanda relations, the candidate withdrawal and the Romanian-candidate maneuvering will likely produce a few more headlines as the OIF leadership question is formally resolved or tabled. Probable: at least one more diplomatic statement or presser from either Kinshasa or Kigali in the coming days. Unlikely: a full diplomatic rupture or a new border incident within this specific week, though the tension is clearly elevated.

Sports and culture will provide a lighter counterpoint. Almost certain: the CAN qualifier results against Comoros and Sierra Leone will be reported, with possible qualification implications. The national-hero designation for Étienne Tshisekedi will continue to generate opinion pieces.

Less likely surprises: a major power outage or fuel crisis in Kinshasa triggered by the Ebola-related mining furloughs; a surprise cabinet reshuffle as Tshisekedi consolidates ahead of the referendum; a new cholera cluster confirmed in a major city; a military coup attempt or mutiny in the east inspired by the death sentences. I would not bet on: a ceasefire announcement in the east; a sudden collapse of the Ebola curve; Tshisekedi calling the referendum for December; a new war with Rwanda; or a major international summit dedicated solely to the Congo crisis.
emoji_reasons: The Ebola outbreak surpassing 11,000 cases and 5,387 deaths, with MSF calling it out of control after six months, is the single most consequential story of the week.
President Tshisekedi signing the referendum law that paves the way for a new Constitution and a third term is the biggest political development, reshaping the country's power structure.
Sixty-six soldiers sentenced to death for cowardice, ADF rebels killing dozens of civilians, and ongoing multi-front fighting in the east make armed conflict the third pillar of this week.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs taken five days apart, several threads grew noticeably. Ebola moved from being a terrifying but still-managed outbreak to one that MSF openly declared out of control, with cases surging past 11,000 and deaths climbing to 5,387. The economic footprint of the virus expanded from a footnote to a visible force: Barrick Gold furloughed workers at its Congo mine, commodity traders began factoring the outbreak into deal-making, and the CDC and Africa CDC flagged attacks on health workers as a structural problem. Armed violence in the east also intensified. The single 33-killing raid in the first photo became a week in which ADF rebels killed between 22 and 66 civilians, including three health workers, and the military responded with a dramatic escalation of discipline by sentencing 66 soldiers to death for cowardice and revolt. M23 activity surfaced, confirming a multi-front war rather than a single ADF problem. Politically, the thread grew from a Senate vote into a presidential signature: Tshisekedi signed the contested referendum law into force, and the government pushed a broader symbolic campaign to erase Kabila's name from streets and to enshrine Étienne Tshisekedi as a national hero, while Lambert Mende, a former Kabila ally, publicly switched sides. The DRC-Rwanda rivalry, which was background noise in the first photo, moved to the foreground at the Francophonie summit, where Kinshasa proposed withdrawing its candidate and backing a Romanian rival to block Kigali. Cholera reappeared as a confirmed parallel epidemic. New threads that had no presence in the first photo include the AI coders rescuing war-lost school records, the domestic minerals-transformation industrial push, the Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers, and the funding-gap crisis inside the Ebola response. Threads that shrank or vanished entirely include the specific mining disputes (the fraud inquiry into seized copper and cobalt, the Huayou Cobalt six-million-dollar compensation, the twelve-billion-dollar power-investment search, the US minerals deal working group), the anthrax alert from Virunga, the Lobito Corridor, the beer-transporter taxation by armed groups, and the C64 arrest threat that was expected to produce detentions. The Youth Olympics teenager story and the US sanctions-on-Rwanda discussion also dropped out of the frame.
delta.wind: The Ebola forecast was the strongest call and it landed almost exactly as predicted. The outbreak stayed dominant, case counts rose, MSF and the WHO issued updated figures, the vaccine question moved from clinical-trial green light to Merck urging wider Ervebo deployment, and the intersection with armed violence produced the killing of three health workers by ADF rebels. The one nuance the expectation missed was the economic spillover into mining operations and commodity trading, which was not anticipated. The armed-violence forecast was broadly correct in direction: at least one more ADF attack happened, and the Uvira corridor saw continued tension. The expectation of a small military operation or command change was met in a more dramatic form than predicted, with the 66 death sentences. The beer-transporter taxation thread, however, vanished without a trace. The mining forecast was the weakest hit. The expectation was very specific: arrests from the fraud inquiry, a new Huayou filing, a named investor for the 12B power search, a State Department statement on the US minerals deal. None of those specific events appeared in the second photo. Instead, the mining thread reorganized around different actors and questions: Barrick Gold's precautionary furlough, a tin-deal negotiation, and a broader industrial-policy push to process minerals domestically. The expectation was too anchored to the disputes that were active on the first photo date and failed to anticipate that the Ebola crisis would pull mining coverage toward health-precaution and market-watching stories. The anthrax alert, flagged as possible, did not develop into a human case or a culling announcement and simply disappeared from the headlines. The political forecast captured the referendum-law progression correctly: the Senate adoption became a presidential signature. But the expectation of C64 arrests materializing as a small crisis was not confirmed; instead, the Kabila-related political energy channeled into street renaming, the national-hero push, and Mende's public realignment, which is a softer, more symbolic power play than the expected detentions. The DRC-Rwanda simmering tension was correctly predicted to persist, but it escalated faster and more visibly than expected, becoming the central drama of the Francophonie summit rather than a background note. The cholera toll climbing was predicted and confirmed. The Lobito Corridor, expected to remain low-visibility, vanished entirely. Among the less-likely surprises, none of the listed items (ceasefire, new Ebola cluster in Haut-Katanga, constitutional court ruling, cabinet resignation) appeared. Among the things the forecast said it would not bet on, none materialized either: no civil-war declaration, no Ebola end, no Senate reversal, no US peacekeeping mission, no coup. The main pattern of error is specificity: the expectation over-indexed on the exact disputes and actors named in the first photo (Huayou, the fraud inquiry, the 12B search, C64 arrests) and under-weighted the broader forces that would reorganize those stories (Ebola's economic pull, Tshisekedi's symbolic consolidation, the military's internal discipline crisis). The forecast also under-weighted the Francophonie summit as a stage for the DRC-Rwanda clash, treating it as background when it became a foreground event.
delta.driver: The force pushing DR Congo from the first photograph to the second is a compounding stress that is hitting the state from three directions at once: a health emergency that is now visibly straining the economy and the military's own personnel, a constitutional power grab by Tshisekedi that is converting parliamentary victory into a broader symbolic and institutional consolidation of his presidency, and a multi-front war in the east that is forcing the army into harsher internal discipline while the rebels kill civilians and health workers in growing numbers. These three pressures are not independent; they feed each other. Ebola weakens the state's capacity to project authority, which makes Tshisekedi's need to lock in a third term through the referendum law more urgent and more aggressive. The war in the east, with its death sentences and ADF and M23 activity, gives the government a security rationale for both the constitutional change and the symbolic erasure of Kabila, the man most associated with the previous war era. Meanwhile, the economic ripple of Ebola into mining and commodity markets gives external actors a new lever of influence, and the DRC-Rwanda rivalry finds a new multilateral stage at the Francophonie summit where Kinshasa can project strength without committing troops. The net effect over five days is a country that is consolidating power at the top, tightening military discipline, and absorbing a health shock that is reshaping its economic calendar, all while its eastern border remains a grinding, multi-rebel war that shows no sign of a diplomatic off-ramp.

crystal.reasoning:
I start from the present: DR Congo is being squeezed from three directions simultaneously. Ebola is the gravitational center at 11,000-plus cases and 5,387 deaths, with MSF declaring it out of control after six months, funding gaps widening, and the economic spillover now visible in Barrick Gold's furlough and commodity traders factoring the outbreak into deals. Tshisekedi has signed the contested referendum law into force, converting a parliamentary victory into a constitutional lock-in, and the government is running a symbolic campaign to erase Kabila from streets and enshrine Étienne Tshisekedi as a national hero. In the east, 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death for cowardice, ADF rebels have killed 22 to 66 civilians including three health workers in a single week, and M23 activity confirms a multi-front war. The DRC-Rwanda rivalry just escalated to the foreground at the Francophonie summit, where Kinshasa backed a Romanian candidate to block Kigali's OIF bid.

The motion from the last photograph shows acceleration on every axis: Ebola went from 'manageable' to 'out of control,' the military discipline escalated from a single incident to 66 death sentences, the political thread moved from a Senate vote to a presidential signature plus a broader symbolic consolidation, and the DRC-Rwanda clash moved from background noise to the central drama of a multilateral summit. The mining story reorganized around Ebola precaution and market watching rather than the specific disputes (Huayou, the fraud inquiry, the 12B search) that dominated the prior photo. Cholera is now confirmed as a parallel epidemic competing for the same overwhelmed health system.

The wind tells me my main pattern of error is over-anchoring on specific named actors and disputes from the first photograph while under-weighting the broader forces that reorganize those stories. The Ebola forecast was strong and landed well. The mining forecast was the weakest hit because it was too tied to specific companies and legal cases. The political forecast captured the referendum progression but missed the symbolic campaign (street renaming, national hero push). The DRC-Rwanda rivalry escalated faster and more visibly than expected. The Francophonie summit was under-weighted as a stage. The 'less likely surprises' and 'would not bet on' lists mostly held up, which is reassuring.

Extending each theme along its motion: Ebola will remain dominant, with cases likely climbing toward 12,000-13,000 and deaths toward 5,500-6,000, continued funding-gap discussions, and the economic spillover deepening. The signed referendum law will trigger the next procedural step (timeline announcement, drafting of the new constitution, or a constitutional court challenge), and the symbolic campaign will generate local controversy. The 66 death sentences will ripple through the army with appeals, morale questions, and possibly a visible reaction from the general officer corps. ADF will continue its killing spree, and the killing of health workers will feed directly into the Ebola response narrative. The Francophonie aftermath will produce diplomatic follow-up but probably not a major new escalation. The mining story will continue to be shaped by Ebola precaution rather than the specific disputes that dominated last week.

The compounding stress is the driver: each crisis feeds the others. Ebola weakens the state's capacity, making Tshisekedi's need to lock in a third term more urgent. The war gives a security rationale for the constitutional change and the erasure of Kabila. The economic ripple gives external actors a new lever. The net effect is a country consolidating power at the top, tightening military discipline, absorbing a health shock, and fighting a grinding multi-rebel war that shows no diplomatic off-ramp.

Where the motion makes less-likely surprises more probable: a constitutional court challenge to the now-signed law becomes procedurally possible and politically motivated; another ADF attack on a health facility is almost a matter of when not whether given three health workers were already killed; the death sentences producing a visible mutiny or mass appeal is more likely than it would be in a calmer army; Rwanda's diplomatic retaliation after being blocked at the Francophonie is a natural next step. I would not bet on a coup, a ceasefire, Tshisekedi resigning, a general strike, the Senate reversing the law, or a US peacekeeping mission.
crystal.forecast:

Cases will likely climb into the 12,000-to-13,000 range, and the death toll will push toward 5,500 or higher. MSF and the WHO will issue updated figures and continued warnings about the outbreak being out of control. The funding-gap narrative will persist, with at least one new report or statement highlighting missing or unspent millions. The parallel cholera epidemic will remain in the headlines as a competing demand on the same overwhelmed health system, and there is a reasonable chance of a report on how the two diseases are interacting in the same treatment centers. The killing of three health workers by ADF rebels last week will feed directly into the Ebola response narrative, and I would not be surprised by at least one more attack on a medical team or facility in the east. Merck's push for wider Ervebo deployment will generate at least one policy or procurement update. The CDC and Africa CDC will likely issue a joint or separate statement on the response. Confidence: high that Ebola stays dominant and the numbers climb; medium on the specific economic spillover stories.

CONSTITUTIONAL CONSOLIDATION AND THE SYMBOLIC CAMPAIGN. Tshisekedi has signed the referendum law, and the next step is procedural: the government will likely announce a timeline for the referendum or begin the drafting process for the new constitution. I am moderately confident that some official statement or cabinet-level announcement will appear this week setting the stage for the referendum. The symbolic campaign will continue: more street and place renamings removing Kabila's name will be reported, generating local controversy and at least one visible protest or public debate. The push to make Étienne Tshisekedi a national hero will generate more coverage, with the opposition and possibly the Catholic Church pushing back. Lambert Mende's public realignment will be referenced in political analysis pieces as evidence of Tshisekedi's widening coalition. The C64 opposition will issue at least one statement reacting to the signed law, but I do not expect a general strike or a mass rally; their energy is more likely to channel into legal challenges and public debate. There is a less-likely but motion-supported surprise: a constitutional court challenge to the referendum law, filed by the opposition or by a group of senators, which would be procedurally possible now that the law is signed. I would put that at roughly 15 to 20 percent. Confidence: medium-high that consolidation continues and the symbolic campaign generates news; medium on the specific form of opposition reaction.

EASTERN WAR AND MILITARY DISCIPLINE. The 66 death sentences for cowardice and revolt will ripple through the armed forces this week. I expect at least one report on the soldiers' reactions, their families' appeals, or a general officer's statement on the sentencing. There is a chance, maybe 10 to 15 percent, of a visible mutiny, a mass appeal, or a junior officer's public dissent, but the more likely outcome is a grinding internal debate about morale and discipline. ADF rebels will continue their killing spree in the east; given they killed 22 to 66 civilians last week, I would expect at least one more significant attack, and the death toll for the week will be in the double or triple digits. The multi-front nature of the war (ADF, M23, FRN remnants) will be confirmed by at least one report on M23 activity in a specific area. The killing of health workers by ADF will be explicitly linked to the Ebola response in media coverage. The government may announce a new military operation or a command change in response to the losses, but I would not bet on a major offensive. Confidence: medium-high for continued ADF violence and the death-sentence ripple; medium for a specific military operation announcement.

DRC-RWANDA RIVALRY AND DIPLOMATIC AFTERMATH. The Francophonie summit clash will produce diplomatic follow-up this week. Rwanda will likely issue a statement or a diplomatic note reacting to being blocked on the OIF leadership, and Kinshasa will respond. The Romanian candidate's status will be a point of reference in coverage. I do not expect a major new escalation beyond statements and diplomatic notes, but the rivalry will stay in the news as a recurring thread. There is a less-likely surprise, maybe 15 percent, of a new bilateral diplomatic note or a recall of an ambassador, but the more likely form is a public sparring match in the press. Confidence: medium that the rivalry stays in the news; lower for a major new event.

MINING AND THE ECONOMY. The mining story will continue to be shaped by Ebola precaution and market watching rather than the specific legal disputes that dominated last week. Barrick Gold's furlough will be referenced, and at least one other mining or commodity operation will be visible in the news. The domestic minerals-transformation industrial push will generate at least one policy or investment story. The tin-deal negotiation may progress or be reported on. I should not anchor to specific named companies or disputes (that is where the last forecast was weakest). The $12B power investment search may resurface, but I would not bet on a named investor appearing this week. Confidence: medium for continued economic stories; lower for specific named events.

LIGHTER THREADS. The ACN qualifiers will produce at least one match report or a national team update. The AI coders rescuing school records story may get a follow-up or a small feature. These are low-stakes but will keep the country visible in the sports and tech sections. Confidence: high that at least one of these appears.

crystal.tldr: DR Congo's week will be dominated by the Ebola crisis as cases climb past 12,000 and the economic spillover into mining deepens, while Tshisekedi's signed third-term law triggers the next procedural steps and a symbolic campaign to erase Kabila from public life. crystal.eli5:
DR Congo is having a really hard week, and next week will not be much better. The Ebola outbreak is the biggest story: more than 11,000 people have been sick and over 5,000 have died. Doctors say the outbreak is still out of control, and now even the big gold mines are pausing work to keep their workers safe. On top of Ebola, cholera is also spreading, so hospitals are dealing with two diseases at the same time with the same tired staff.

Politically, the president just signed a law that lets him run for a third term in office, which many people think is a stretch of the rules. His government is also renaming streets to remove the name of the former president, which is like erasing someone from the map. The opposition is angry but probably will not do anything as dramatic as a general strike; they will more likely go to the courts or give speeches.

In the eastern part of the country, rebels called the ADF have been killing civilians, including three health workers who were trying to treat Ebola patients. The army responded by giving 66 of its own soldiers the death penalty for what it called cowardice in battle, which is a very harsh punishment and is making other soldiers nervous. The war is not just against one group; there are at least two or three different rebel forces fighting in different areas, and there is no sign of a peace deal coming soon.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A correctly identified Ebola as the dominant story and predicted updated case counts showing increases, which materialized with cases passing 11,000 and 5,387 deaths. Its prediction that the intersection of Ebola and armed violence would generate dramatic incidents was well supported by the ADF killing civilians including three health workers. The military section's prediction of 'a small operation or a change of command in the east' is the closest any forecast came to the week's biggest military story: 66 soldiers sentenced to death for cowardice and revolt before FRN rebels. This is not exactly a 'change of command,' but it is a dramatic military-administrative decision in the same register, and A at least pointed toward a significant internal military development rather than a new offensive. The referendum law prediction was a strong hit: A expected either a presidential decree or fresh opposition protests, and Tshisekedi signed the law, generating major coverage. The DRC-Rwanda tension 'simmering in the background of any diplomatic event' was directionally right for the Francophonie summit clash, though A understated how prominent it would be. Cholera was correctly flagged as continuing to climb. The mining section was more specific than B's (fraud inquiry producing an arrest, Huayou legal filing, US minerals working group meeting), but none of those specific events appeared in the headlines; instead, mining showed up through Barrick furloughing employees and a metals trader tin deal, which is more Ebola-adjacent than dispute-adjacent. The anthrax prediction did not materialize. The C64 arrest prediction did not appear in the headlines, though Kabila-related stories (street renaming, Mende's defection) kept the political axis alive. The 'things not to bet on' list was entirely correct. Overall, A captured the broad shape well, with its strongest specific hit being the military dimension and the referendum law, and its weakest being the mining specifics that did not play out as described.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B was more precise on the Ebola story, which was the week's dominant thread. Its prediction of the death toll reaching 'mid-5,000s to low 6,000s' landed accurately at 5,387. Its specific call that MSF would push harder for wider Ervebo access and that the funding gap would be a recurring frustration was directly confirmed by MSF declaring the outbreak out of control, the CDC and Africa CDC flagging attacks on health workers, and the coverage of nearly a billion dollars in funding with visible gaps. The framing of 'not one disease but a health system under siege from three directions' was well supported by the simultaneous Ebola, cholera, and (referenced) anthrax coverage. The intersection-of-crises theme was explicitly articulated and well supported: Bloomberg's headline 'Ebola, a Rebellion and Now a Constitutional Gamble in Congo' is exactly the kind of multi-crisis tie-together B predicted, and the ADF killing health workers is a direct security-health intersection. The Francophonie prediction was a notable miss in scale: B called it 'a minor diplomatic footnote rather than a major story,' yet it generated at least four to five headlines, with DRC proposing to withdraw its candidate and back a Romanian to block Rwanda. This was a significant multilateral confrontation, not a footnote. The security section correctly identified ADF as the primary threat and the FRN as political context, and the observation that 'Kabila is receding as a military actor and rising as a political target' is actually well supported by the week's Kabila-erasure stories (street renaming, Mende's defection, the national hero controversy). However, B did not specifically anticipate the 66 death sentences, which was the week's most dramatic military story. The mining section was less specific than A's and also mostly missed: the fraud inquiry, Huayou, and Trafigura references did not appear in headlines. The C64 arrest was predicted as the 'sharpest political thread' but did not materialize in the headlines. The British doctor follow-up and the new Ebola case in a third country did not appear. The 'things not to bet on' list was entirely correct. Overall, B was stronger on the dominant Ebola story and the intersection framing, but weaker on the Francophonie scale and the specific military development.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts captured the broad shape of the week correctly: Ebola dominant, violence in the east continuing, the referendum law as a major political event, DRC-Rwanda tension surfacing at the Francophonie, cholera as a secondary health story, and mining as a background theme. Both correctly avoided the big surprises (no coup, no Ebola containment, no civil war declaration, no volcanic event). The main differentiators cut in different directions. B was more precise and specific on the Ebola story, which was the week's biggest thread: the death toll range, the MSF/Ervebo push, the funding gap frustration, and the multi-disease framing all landed more accurately than A's broader 'WHO and MSF will issue updated counts' language. B's explicit intersection-of-crises theme was well supported by the actual coverage, particularly the Bloomberg headline tying Ebola, rebellion, and constitutional politics together. A, on the other hand, had a notably better handle on the military dimension. Its prediction of 'a small operation or a change of command in the east' is the closest any forecast came to the 66 soldiers sentenced to death, which was a multi-headline story and arguably the week's most dramatic single event. B's security section focused on ADF raids and the FRN as political context, which is relevant but does not capture the regular army's internal disciplinary drama as well. On the Francophonie, A's 'background of any diplomatic event' is an underestimate, but B's 'minor diplomatic footnote rather than a major story' is a more specific and more wrong characterization, given the four or five headlines the summit generated. On mining, A was more specific (fraud inquiry arrest, Huayou filing, US working group) but all three specific predictions missed; B was vaguer and also missed, so neither had an edge there. The Kabila-related political stories (street renaming, Mende's defection, national hero controversy) were not specifically predicted by either, though B's framing of Kabila as 'rising as a political target' is closer to the street-renaming and Mende stories than A's focus on C64 arrests. The C64 arrest, predicted by both as a likely event, did not appear in the headlines, which is a shared miss. Weighing everything: B's superior precision on the dominant story (Ebola) and its well-supported intersection framing give it an edge on the story that mattered most. A's edge on the military dimension (the 66 death sentences) is real but that was one major story among many, and A's mining specifics, while more detailed, all missed. B's Francophonie underestimate is a blemish but not as consequential as getting the Ebola details wrong would have been. The two forecasts are close, but B served a reader slightly better as a picture of the coming week because it was more accurate on the thread that dominated coverage and offered a more useful analytical frame (intersection of crises) that the actual headlines confirmed. VERDICT: B
